arguments.content:
This chapter introduces production systems: the people, equipment, and procedures a company organizes to manufacture products. A production system has two main parts: facilities and manufacturing support. Facilities include the factory, machines, tools, material-handling and inspection equipment, computer controls, and the layout that groups equipment and workers into manufacturing systems. Depending on human involvement, work may be manual, shared between worker and machine, or automated. Automation can be partial or full; people remain important for supervision, adjustments, maintenance, and responding to problems. Humans are especially valuable for learning, adapting, and handling unfamiliar situations, while machines excel at consistent repetition, speed, strength, and data storage.

Manufacturing support systems plan and manage production without directly handling the product. Four connected functions are business activities, product design, manufacturing planning, and manufacturing control. Business teams receive customer orders and forecast demand. Design defines the product. Planning determines the operations, schedules products and materials, and checks that workforce and equipment capacity can meet demand. Control monitors factory progress, inventory, and product quality, using inspection and problem-solving methods.

The chapter then explains automation across both factory operations and support work. Automated manufacturing systems can process, assemble, inspect, and move products. Fixed automation uses dedicated equipment for very high-volume production, offering speed but little variety. Programmable automation changes instructions and setup to make different products, typically in batches at lower or medium volumes. Flexible automation makes product changes with little or no changeover time, allowing mixed production. Finally, computer-integrated manufacturing links business, design, planning, and factory control through computers. CAD supports design, CAM supports manufacturing engineering, and CAD/CAM connects the two. The central idea is that effective manufacturing depends on coordinating people, physical facilities, information, and the appropriate level of automation.

This chapter explains how a production system brings together people, equipment, and procedures to make products. It has two main parts: factory facilities and manufacturing support systems. Facilities include machines, tools, material handling and inspection equipment, computer controls, and the factory layout. Work can be performed manually, by a worker using powered equipment, or by automated systems. Automation may be partial or full, but people continue to supervise, adjust, maintain, and handle unexpected problems. People are adaptable and learn from experience; machines are consistent, fast, powerful, and able to store and retrieve data.

Manufacturing support systems coordinate the work through four connected functions. Business activities receive customer orders and forecast demand. Product design defines what is to be made. Manufacturing planning selects processes, schedules products and materials, and checks that available workers and equipment can meet the plan. Manufacturing control monitors work on the factory floor, inventory, and quality, using inspection and problem-solving methods.

The chapter distinguishes three kinds of automation. Fixed automation uses specialized equipment for very high-volume production, with high speed but little flexibility. Programmable automation changes machine instructions and setup to make different products, usually in batches. Flexible automation can switch among product types with very little changeover time, supporting varied production. Finally, computer-integrated manufacturing uses computers to connect business, design, planning, and factory operations. CAD assists product design; CAM supports manufacturing engineering; CAD/CAM links these activities. The key message is that efficient manufacturing depends on coordinating people, facilities, information, and the right degree of automation.
